area: Area VI. Flight by Reference to Instruments
objective: By the end of this lesson you can explain how pitch, bank and power work together in straight-and-level flight, teach it with either the control-and-performance or the primary-and-supporting method on round dials and on glass, full panel and partial panel, coach coordination and trim, fly it to instrument standards while explaining it, and analyze and correct the common errors an examiner simulates.
why: Once a pilot learns the role of each instrument, he or she is better equipped to control the airplane when one or more key instruments fail [[23:135|IFH 6-2]]. In an instrument failure, avoiding an upset may depend on the pilot's skill with secondary instruments and partial panel flying [[24:107|AFH 5-2]]. The CFII PTS stresses this because of fatal spatial disorientation accidents of instrument-rated pilots flying in cloud with failed gyros or a lost electronic display [[FAA-S-8081-9E:16|PTS Emphasis on Attitude Instrument Flying and Partial Panel Skills]]. Straight-and-level is where your student first learns to read each instrument on its own, so it is where that safety net is built.

warmup: Think first: your instrument student holds altitude within 20 feet on the PFD. You simulate an AHRS failure, and within a minute she is 250 feet low, 30° off heading and staring at the altitude tape. Which skill was missing all along, and what would you change in her full panel lessons?

chunks.title: What the examiner looks for in Area VI

body.p: **Teaching straight-and-level flight** is the base of Area VI. The Area NOTE says the evaluator selects Task H (unusual attitudes) and at least one other Task, and you select either the primary and supporting or the control and performance method for teaching the Area [[FAA-S-8081-9E:32|PTS Area VI NOTE]].

The PTS says Area VI must be taught under both full panel and backup or partial panel instruments, and the evaluator should determine that you fully understand the method you chose [[FAA-S-8081-9E:17|PTS Emphasis on Attitude Instrument Flying and Partial Panel Skills]]. The reason: many light airplanes flown in IMC have a single vacuum source and no dual gyros, and backup instruments in technically advanced airplanes may sit away from the pilot's direct view [[FAA-S-8081-9E:16|PTS Emphasis on Attitude Instrument Flying and Partial Panel Skills]].

Your explanations follow the teaching methods of the Aviation Instructor's Handbook, including scenario-based lessons, SRM evaluation and learner-centered grading [[FAA-S-8081-9E:10|PTS Use of the PTS]]
"Demonstrates and simultaneously explains"
The explanation is clear, concise, technically accurate and complete, with no prompting; failing that is a typical reason for an unsatisfactory [[FAA-S-8081-9E:15|PTS Unsatisfactory Performance]]

You recognize, analyze and correct errors the evaluator flies; the evaluator will not simulate any condition that may jeopardize safe flight [[FAA-S-8081-9E:14|PTS Evaluator Responsibility]] [[FAA-S-8081-9E:10|PTS Use of the PTS]]
Your own flying

Procedures flown to the instrument pilot skill level while giving effective instruction; failing that is also a typical reason for an unsatisfactory [[FAA-S-8081-9E:15|PTS Unsatisfactory Performance]]

body.p: Your choice of method does not shrink what you must know. Both methods use the same instruments and the same control responses; they differ in how much they rely on the attitude indicator and how the other instruments are interpreted [[23:135|IFH 6-2]] [[23:149|IFH 6-16]].

callout.text: The rule: to give instrument training toward an instrument rating, a flight instructor needs an instrument rating on the flight instructor certificate appropriate to the aircraft [[60:346|14 CFR 61.195(c)(1)]].

body.p: Related lessons: the Instrument lesson IR.IV.A covers the pilot's side of these maneuvers, the CFI lesson AI.XI.A covers basic attitude flying for VFR learners, and IR.VII.D covers the partial panel approach. This lesson adds both methods, round dials and glass, partial panel, and how to teach and fix it.

callout.text: Application: be fluent in both methods. Your future students may have learned the other one, and the examiner may ask how it differs.

check.q: The examiner asks which method you will use, then asks you to explain the other one. Is that a fair question?
check.a: Yes. You pick one method and must fully understand it [[FAA-S-8081-9E:32|PTS Area VI NOTE]] [[FAA-S-8081-9E:17|PTS Emphasis on Attitude Instrument Flying and Partial Panel Skills]], but both methods use the same instruments and control responses [[23:135|IFH 6-2]], and the evaluator checks your ability to instruct students at various stages of training and levels of experience [[FAA-S-8081-9E:10|PTS Use of the PTS]].

chunks.title: Pitch, bank and power: how they work together

body.p: **The relationship of pitch, bank, and power in straight-and-level flight.** In level flight the pitch attitude varies with airspeed and load, and in small airplanes load can normally be ignored for training. At a constant airspeed there is only one pitch attitude for level flight: nose-high at slow cruise, nose-low at fast cruise [[23:163|IFH 7-2]].

Power decides what that attitude produces. At any given airspeed, the power setting decides whether the airplane is level, climbing or descending; if altitude is held constant, power decides the airspeed [[23:169|IFH 7-8]]. The IFH calls it "power and attitude equal performance": the same picture at full power gives 500 fpm at 90 knots in a small airplane and 2,000 fpm at 250 knots in a jet [[23:146|IFH 6-13]].

Bank: with the wings level and the airplane coordinated, the flightpath is straight [[23:167|IFH 7-6]]. In coordinated flight a bank produces a turn, so the heading indicator shows bank indirectly, and a fast-moving card means a large bank [[23:168|IFH 7-7]].

body.p: The three move together during any power change. Added power makes the pitch instruments show a climb unless forward pressure is used, and the airplane yaws and rolls left unless aileron and rudder counter it. As airspeed decreases, a proportionate increase in pitch is needed to hold altitude [[23:170|IFH 7-9]] [[23:172|IFH 7-11]].

callout.text: Application: teach it as a trade. The IFH says to think of altitude and airspeed as interchangeable: lower the nose to trade altitude for airspeed, raise it to convert airspeed to altitude [[23:169|IFH 7-8]]. Have the student say "pitch, power or both?" before each correction.

check.q: Your student is 100 feet high and 10 knots fast. She lowers the nose a little and nothing else. What happens, and what should she do?
check.a: Lowering the nose trades altitude for even more airspeed [[23:169|IFH 7-8]]. With both altitude and airspeed high, both pitch and power must change [[23:170|IFH 7-9]].

chunks.title: Control and performance, taught from the right seat

body.p: The control and performance method controls attitude and power, as needed, to produce the performance wanted [[23:135|IFH 6-2]]. It splits the panel into three groups:

head: Group
Round dials
Glass (PFD)
rows: Control
Attitude indicator and power indicators such as manifold pressure, tachometer and fuel flow, calibrated for precise steps [[23:135|IFH 6-2]]
Attitude indicator, manifold pressure and tachometer; all three reflect small adjustments [[23:151|IFH 6-18]]
Performance
Altimeter, airspeed indicator, VSI [[23:135|IFH 6-2]]
The same, plus heading, pitch attitude and the slip/skid indicator [[23:152|IFH 6-19]]
Navigation
Course, range and glideslope indicators, bearing pointers [[23:135|IFH 6-2]]
GPS, VOR/NDB, moving map, localizer and glideslope [[23:152|IFH 6-19]]

body.p: The control instruments do not tell how fast or how high the airplane is; for that the pilot reads the performance instruments [[23:152|IFH 6-19]]. The four steps:

bullets: 1. Establish attitude and power on the control instruments. Knowing approximate pitch and power settings reduces the workload [[23:135|IFH 6-2]] [[23:152|IFH 6-19]] [[23:153|IFH 6-20]].

2. Trim until control pressures are neutralized; hands-off trim is essential for smooth, precise control [[23:135|IFH 6-2]]. Poor trim is one of the most common errors instructors see in instrument students [[23:153|IFH 6-20]].
3. Cross-check the performance instruments: see and interpret, and decide how much and which way to adjust [[23:136|IFH 6-3]].
4. Adjust in small increments: pitch in bar widths, bank on the roll scale, power on the tachometer or manifold pressure. A common error is a bigger change than needed [[23:153|IFH 6-20]].

body.p: The IFH sums it up: the keys are setting the attitude on the attitude indicator and the engine output on the power instruments, and cross-checking is the vital ingredient [[23:154|IFH 6-21]].

callout.text: Application: when you teach this method partial panel, say what stands in for the missing control instrument. With the attitude indicator gone, pitch is controlled by the rate of change on the altimeter or altitude tape and its trend [[23:165|IFH 7-4]] [[23:197|IFH 7-36]], and bank by the turn coordinator's miniature airplane [[23:168|IFH 7-7]].

check.q: A student using control and performance sees the altimeter creeping down. Where does she make the correction?
check.a: On the control instrument: a small pitch change on the attitude indicator, then trim, then cross-check again [[23:136|IFH 6-3]] [[23:140|IFH 6-7]].

chunks.title: Primary and supporting, taught from the right seat

body.p: This method groups the instruments by control function: pitch, bank, power and trim [[23:137|IFH 6-4]]. The primary instrument gives the most pertinent information for that part of the maneuver and is usually the one held constant; the others help keep it there [[23:143|IFH 6-10]] [[23:167|IFH 7-6]]. On glass, all attitude changes are still made on the attitude indicator and the power instruments [[23:154|IFH 6-21]].

body.p: One phase changes the pitch primary: while returning to an altitude, the VSI is the primary pitch instrument [[23:166|IFH 7-5]] [[23:198|IFH 7-37]].

Two points examiners like to probe. First, the method does not devalue the attitude indicator: it is the only instrument that instantly and directly shows the actual attitude, and it should always be used when available [[23:143|IFH 6-10]]. Second, which instrument is primary for pitch depends on the airplane, the weather, the pilot's experience and other factors; the IFH normally treats the altimeter as primary in level flight [[23:167|IFH 7-6]]. On glass, the IFH says the attitude indicator is primary only when flying a specific pitch or bank angle; otherwise it is a control instrument [[23:199|IFH 7-38]].

callout.text: Level flight: Altimeter = pitch, Heading = bank, Airspeed = power. Returning to altitude: VSI = pitch. Throttle moving: power gauge = power.

check.q: Halfway through a slowdown from 120 to 100 knots, with the throttle at the underpower setting, your student says the airspeed indicator is primary for power. Is she right?
check.a: Not at that moment. While the power is reduced to the underpower value, the manifold pressure gauge is momentarily primary; as the airspeed nears 100 knots and power is reset, the airspeed indicator is primary again [[23:172|IFH 7-11]].

chunks.title: Full panel on round dials: pitch and bank technique

body.p: **Procedure using full panel** on analog instruments starts on the ground and at the first level-off. As soon as practical in level flight at cruise, set the miniature aircraft's wings in front of the horizon bar; do not move it for other speeds, so the attitude indicator shows a true picture in all maneuvers [[23:138|IFH 6-5]]. The wings and center dot represent about 2° of pitch [[23:114|IFH 5-19]].

head: Pitch item
IFH technique
rows: Drill
Hold the horizon bar at a half, one, then one-and-a-half bar widths [[23:164|IFH 7-3]]
Size of correction
Under 100 ft: half a bar width. Over 100 ft: an initial full bar width [[23:165|IFH 7-4]]
Two steps
First a change to stop the needle, then a change to return to altitude [[23:165|IFH 7-4]]
Rate of return
About double the error, never more than the airplane's optimum climb or descent rate [[23:166|IFH 7-5]]
Overcontrolling
More than 200 fpm away from the rate wanted [[23:139|IFH 6-6]]
VSI lag
Grows with the speed and size of the pitch change; a big, abrupt change gives erratic needle movement and a reverse indication [[23:166|IFH 7-5]]. An IVSI shows little or no lag [[23:139|IFH 6-6]]
VSI out of calibration
Use its level-flight reading as zero [[23:166|IFH 7-5]] [[23:167|IFH 7-6]]

body.p: Bank: correct heading with a bank no greater than the degrees to turn, and never more than a standard-rate bank [[23:168|IFH 7-7]]. Small banks are hard to see on a three-inch attitude indicator, especially when leaning or shifting in the seat, so check the bank scale pointer [[23:167|IFH 7-6]] [[23:168|IFH 7-7]]. The attitude indicator's precession error makes a precise heading check necessary [[23:168|IFH 7-7]]. Keep the turn coordinator's miniature airplane in the scan and correct even the smallest deviation with very light pressure [[23:169|IFH 7-8]].

Know the instrument's limits: on some attitude indicators the bank scale moves opposite to the bank, so read direction from the miniature aircraft [[1:221|PHAK 8-19]]. Small pitch and bank errors can follow rapid acceleration, deceleration or a 180° turn and correct themselves within a minute or so [[23:114|IFH 5-19]].

callout.text: Two demonstrations from the IFH: compare normal pitch corrections on the attitude indicator with the natural horizon, then show a hurried big correction for a nose-down error that overshoots nose-high, followed by the slower, smoother correction that gets back sooner [[23:164|IFH 7-3]] [[23:165|IFH 7-4]].

check.q: On round dials your student is 150 feet low. What pitch change and rate do you coach?
check.a: An initial full bar width, because the error is over 100 feet [[23:165|IFH 7-4]], for about 300 fpm, double the error, as long as that is within the airplane's optimum rate [[23:166|IFH 7-5]].

chunks.title: Full panel on glass: what changes on a PFD

body.p: **Procedure using full panel** on a PFD uses the same ideas with finer marks. The attitude display spans the screen, the pitch scale is marked every 5° so pitch can be set to about half a degree, and a yellow chevron replaces the miniature airplane [[23:153|IFH 6-20]]. The AHRS sets the chevron's position at start-up; there is no need or means to adjust it [[23:155|IFH 6-22]]. The full height of the chevron is about 5° [[23:196|IFH 7-35]].

No lag from the digital air data computer [[23:197|IFH 7-36]]

Trend vectors, 6 seconds on the IFH example; a supplement, not the main pitch reference [[23:159|IFH 6-26]] [[23:160|IFH 6-27]]

body.p: The PFD attitude display shows pitch, not altitude, so a pilot should not try to hold level flight with it alone [[23:196|IFH 7-35]]. With altitude constant, the IFH notes that the VSI and altitude trend indications are not shown; when they appear, pitch has changed [[23:155|IFH 6-22]] [[23:156|IFH 6-23]]. Two causes of altitude deviation are turbulence and momentary distractions [[23:155|IFH 6-22]].

Scan: the radial scan suits the PFD because the extended horizon keeps pitch in peripheral vision. Start at the chevron, go up to the roll pointer and slip/skid indicator, back, left to airspeed, back, right to altitude, back, down to heading, back [[23:157|IFH 6-24]] [[23:158|IFH 6-25]]. Add the engine indications and the standby instruments, using a modified radial scan if data are on the MFD [[23:157|IFH 6-24]] [[23:159|IFH 6-26]].

callout.text: Precision invites fixation. Digital readouts tempt pilots to chase the exact power setting [[23:154|IFH 6-21]], and tapes tempt them to hold airspeed to one knot, which is unnecessary [[23:161|IFH 6-28]].

check.q: Your glass student is 60 feet low and asks how much to raise the chevron. What do you say?
check.a: About 1°, a fifth of the chevron's thickness [[23:197|IFH 7-36]], for roughly 120 fpm, twice the deviation and under the 500 fpm cap [[23:155|IFH 6-22]].

chunks.title: Partial panel on round dials: the vacuum failure

body.p: **Procedure using partial panel** on analog instruments: except the instrument takeoff, every basic maneuver in the IFH can be flown with the attitude gyro and heading indicator covered or inoperative [[23:162|IFH 7-1]]. Gyros run on separate electric or pneumatic sources so one failure does not take everything, and many airplanes with vacuum attitude indicators use electric rate instruments, or the reverse [[23:112|IFH 5-17]]. Have the student find each instrument's power source in the POH/AFM [[23:114|IFH 5-19]].

Recognition comes first. A warning flag, or an inconsistency between the attitude indicator and the supporting performance instruments, usually identifies the failure. Keep control, speed up the cross-check, and compare the attitude indicator with the turn indicator and VSI, which compares the suction, static and electrical systems [[23:332|IFH 11-7]]. Vacuum gyros can fail slowly and wander as they spin down; in Figure 11-8 the airplane is actually level at 2,000 feet, not turning left as the failed gyros suggest [[23:332|IFH 11-7]].

Altimeter: the needle's rate shows the size of the pitch error. VSI: the trend first, then the rate. Airspeed: a fast change means a big pitch change

body.p: Teach the pitch skill alone first. To practice without an attitude indicator, make small pitch changes by the natural horizon and watch the altimeter: find the change that gives the slowest steady rate, then practice controlling that rate [[23:165|IFH 7-4]]. Then cover the gyros. Covering failed instruments may help a pilot keep control and navigate; the next step is usually to advise ATC and, if needed, declare an emergency [[23:332|IFH 11-7]].
Many small airplanes have no vacuum warning system, so the suction gauge belongs in the scan [[23:332|IFH 11-7]] [[23:333|IFH 11-8]] [[1:224|PHAK 8-22]].

callout.text: A vacuum failure can lead an unsuspecting pilot into a dangerous unusual attitude, so pilots must practice flying without the attitude and heading indicators [[23:333|IFH 11-8]]. The AFH gives the example of a fatigued pilot in night IMC with a vacuum pump failure who could become disoriented and lose control in extended, unpracticed partial panel flight [[24:108|AFH 5-3]].

check.q: Under the hood your student's attitude indicator shows a slow left bank, but the turn coordinator is level, the ball centered and the VSI at zero. What do you teach?
check.a: That inconsistency is how a failure is identified: compare the attitude indicator with the turn indicator and VSI, identify the failed gyro, fly on the instruments that still work, and cover the failed one [[23:332|IFH 11-7]].

chunks.title: Partial panel on glass: AHRS failure and standby instruments

body.p: **Procedure using partial panel** on an electronic display means the AHRS is simulated or rendered inoperative; again every maneuver except the instrument takeoff can be flown that way [[23:194|IFH 7-33]]. In the IFH example an AHRS failure removes all attitude and heading from the PFD and all unusual attitude protection, and the autopilot keeps only roll and altitude hold. The slip/skid indicator goes too, and that airplane has no standby turn coordinator [[23:217|IFH 7-56]].

The standby instruments: an airspeed indicator, attitude indicator, altimeter and magnetic compass are installed for use when the PFD is unavailable [[23:331|IFH 11-6]]. They need no electrical power or, like many attitude indicators, carry their own battery [[23:149|IFH 6-16]]. The analog standby attitude indicator can tumble in extreme pitch or bank [[23:219|IFH 7-58]]. Note where they sit in Figure 11-7: low in the center panel, the kind of backup the PTS says may not be directly in front of the pilot [[FAA-S-8081-9E:16|PTS Emphasis on Attitude Instrument Flying and Partial Panel Skills]].

bullets: Pitch from the altitude tape and trend indicator alone; avoid abrupt yoke movements, which give large pitch changes and a bigger departure from altitude [[23:197|IFH 7-36]].
Two actions: a smooth input to stop the tape, then a pitch change back toward the altitude [[23:197|IFH 7-36]].
About 1° of pitch for deviations under 100 feet [[23:197|IFH 7-36]].
Rapid control movements set up an oscillation that can disorient the pilot and fixate him or her on altitude, costing directional control as well [[23:197|IFH 7-36]].
Heading: after an AHRS or magnetometer failure the compass gives heading; timed turns are simpler than compass turns [[23:214|IFH 7-53]].
Autopilot: in the IFH example, after an AHRS and ADC failure the manufacturer recommends the wing leveler to cut workload [[23:219|IFH 7-58]].

body.p: Two system facts to teach. Many light glass airplanes feed the backup instruments from the same pitot-static sources, so one blockage can fail both, and glass failure indications are not standardized [[24:364|AFH 18-15]]. An alternator failure in a technically advanced airplane is treated as an emergency. In the IFH example a standby battery powers the essential bus (usually the AHRS, ADC, PFD, nav 1 and com 1) once the main battery runs down to about 19 volts, or when the pilot switches the battery master off, but generally only with the standby battery switch in ARM, which should be set before departure; the AFM has the details [[23:331|IFH 11-6]].

callout.text: Application: on every glass lesson ask, "What is left if the AHRS quits? The ADC? The alternator?" and have the student answer from the AFM supplement. The IFH shows one example system only [[23:217|IFH 7-56]], and failure behavior differs between systems [[24:364|AFH 18-15]].

check.q: Your glass student says she would fly the standby attitude indicator just like the PFD. What differences do you point out?
check.a: It is a small instrument low in the center panel [[23:332|IFH 11-7]], so her scan must move; it can tumble in extreme attitudes [[23:219|IFH 7-58]]; and with the AHRS gone she may also lose heading and the slip/skid indicator on the PFD [[23:217|IFH 7-56]].

body.p: **Coordination of controls and trim.** The ball shows the quality of the turn: off center means a slip or skid, and with the wings level and the airplane properly trimmed it stays centered [[23:169|IFH 7-8]]. On the PFD the slip/skid indicator is the lower part of the split triangle; if it is off to one side, step on the rudder pedal on that side [[23:157|IFH 6-24]]. If the heading is steady but the roll pointer and roll index are not aligned, the airplane is uncoordinated; correct with rudder [[23:200|IFH 7-39]].

bullets: Adding power: the airplane yaws and rolls left unless aileron and rudder counter it, and keeping ahead takes a faster cross-check [[23:170|IFH 7-9]].
Reducing power: be ready for left rudder, back pressure and aileron the instant the pitch and bank instruments show a deviation [[23:172|IFH 7-11]].
Ball left and left wing low: left rudder to center the ball, right aileron to level the wings, cross-check heading and attitude, then retrim [[23:169|IFH 7-8]].
Use balanced power when possible to help keep the airplane coordinated [[23:173|IFH 7-12]].

body.p: Trim: an airplane is correctly trimmed when it holds the desired attitude with all control pressures neutralized, and the skill a pilot develops depends largely on how well he or she learns to keep it trimmed [[23:141|IFH 6-8]]. The order never changes: set the attitude with control pressure, then trim so it holds with the controls released [[23:143|IFH 6-10]] [[23:173|IFH 7-12]].

How
rows: Pitch

Hold the pressure, roll the trim in the direction of the pressure, relax and watch the primary instrument [[23:204|IFH 7-43]]. On glass: release the yoke briefly, note which way the nose goes, reapply pressure and trim toward it; small trim inputs make large pitch changes [[23:196|IFH 7-35]]
Rudder
Rudder trim in the direction the ball is displaced [[23:173|IFH 7-12]]
Aileron
Aileron trim, if fitted, to hold the wings level [[23:143|IFH 6-10]]
Partial panel
Level the turn coordinator's airplane with aileron, center the ball with rudder, release slowly while trimming [[23:169|IFH 7-8]]

body.p: The idea students miss: an airplane is trimmed for an airspeed, not a pitch attitude or altitude. Add 50 rpm at 100 knots and it speeds up, climbs, and settles back at 100 knots at a higher altitude; to hold altitude, forward pressure and forward trim are needed [[23:204|IFH 7-43]].

callout.text: A light touch helps both: thumb and two fingers, not a full fist, which tends to add excess pressure [[23:196|IFH 7-35]]. Trimmed in calm air, the student should be able to let go and hold level flight for long periods; the IFH calls this one of the hardest skills to learn before flying in IMC [[23:196|IFH 7-35]].

check.q: After adding 50 rpm, your student keeps rolling in nose-down trim while the speed is still changing, and the altitude keeps wandering. What is missing?
check.a: Trim sets an airspeed. Before final trimming the airspeed must be held constant; if it keeps changing, the trim is not set properly and the altitude varies [[23:204|IFH 7-43]]. Hold altitude with pressure, let the speed settle, then trim.

chunks.title: Risk: setting up errors and failures safely

body.p: The PTS rule for examiners is a good rule for you: no simulated condition that may jeopardize safe flight or could damage the airplane [[FAA-S-8081-9E:10|PTS Use of the PTS]]. The PTS ties Area VI to spatial disorientation accidents [[FAA-S-8081-9E:16|PTS Emphasis on Attitude Instrument Flying and Partial Panel Skills]]; the AFH counts nearly 200 spatial disorientation accidents from 2008 to 2013, more than 70% of them fatal [[24:108|AFH 5-3]]. Large corrections with rapid attitude changes can bring it on [[23:155|IFH 6-22]].

bullets: Who flies: brief the positive exchange of flight controls before flight, "You have the flight controls," "I have the flight controls," "You have the flight controls," with a visual check [[25:178|AIH 9-8]] [[25:179|AIH 9-9]]. The PTS strongly recommends the same three steps [[FAA-S-8081-9E:16|PTS Positive Exchange of Flight Controls]].
Guard the controls. If needed, take them and calmly announce "I have the flight controls"; anxious learners can be very strong [[25:179|AIH 9-9]].

Lookout: simulated instrument flight needs a qualified safety pilot in the other control seat [[60:446|14 CFR 91.109(c)(1)]], see and avoid applies under IFR or VFR when weather permits [[60:447|14 CFR 91.113(b)]], and the weather should leave extra margin near busy airways and airports [[33:258|AIM 4-3-16]].

Device: on the practical test, the view-limiting device must block the applicant's outside view without blocking the examiner's [[60:225|14 CFR 61.45(d)(2)]]; brief when and how it goes on and off [[FAA-S-8081-9E:12|PTS Other Requirements]].
Failures: the IFH describes partial panel with the gyros covered [[23:162|IFH 7-1]], and on glass with the AHRS simulated or inoperative [[23:194|IFH 7-33]].

Distractions: the PTS requires the evaluator to cause a realistic distraction [[FAA-S-8081-9E:16|PTS Use of Distractions During Practical Tests]]; the AIH lists examples such as resetting the clock or computing true airspeed [[25:180|AIH 9-10]]. Add them only once the task works on its own [[25:81|AIH 3-30]].

body.p: Risk management belongs in the lesson itself. The AIH case study is a pilot who knew his vacuum pump had failed, flew into IMC anyway and lost control; the most effective mitigation may have been to divert and land in VMC [[25:186|AIH 10-2]]. The AIH also suggests instrument pilots consider the risk of an airplane with a single alternator or a single radio and navigation system [[25:189|AIH 10-5]].

callout.text: Application: simulate failures only in VMC, at a safe altitude, with a briefed plan. Stop the exercise the moment traffic, weather or a real abnormality appears, and say clearly when a failure is simulated so the student never confuses training with a real emergency.

check.q: To make it "realistic," a colleague suggests pulling the AHRS breaker in actual IMC on a training flight. What do the sources say?
check.a: The PTS bars examiners from simulating any condition that may jeopardize safe flight [[FAA-S-8081-9E:10|PTS Use of the PTS]], and the AFH notes some failure modes cannot be simulated in training [[24:372|AFH 18-23]]. Simulate in VMC with covers or the method your AFM supplement allows.

body.p: **Common errors related to straight-and-level flight.** For S2 the evaluator flies these errors on purpose. Say what you see, name the error, explain the cause and give the fix, the "recognize, analyze and correct" the PTS asks for [[FAA-S-8081-9E:15|PTS Satisfactory Performance]]. For each error below: the picture, the usual cause, the fix and a way to show it.
**Slow or improper cross-check during straight-and-level flight.**

head: Error
What you see
Usual cause
Fix and how to teach it
rows: Insufficient cross-check of pitch instruments
Airspeed low; the student pushes forward and loses altitude, airspeed still low
Low power, not a nose-high attitude [[23:173|IFH 7-12]] [[23:204|IFH 7-43]]
Speed up the cross-check to all relevant instruments; stabilize airspeed and altitude before an input [[23:205|IFH 7-44]]. Show it by quietly reducing power (Application)
Fixation
A stare at one instrument while others drift: 200 ft low with the heading wandering [[23:146|IFH 6-13]]; on glass, pitch watched while a heading trend grows [[23:205|IFH 7-44]] [[23:206|IFH 7-45]]
Too much importance given to one instrument [[23:205|IFH 7-44]]; often the task has not had enough practice on its own [[25:81|AIH 3-30]]
Spread attention evenly and keep scanning while waiting for a correction to show [[23:205|IFH 7-44]]
Omission
An instrument never checked: heading during power or pitch changes [[23:174|IFH 7-13]]; on glass the standby instruments, compass and slip/skid indicator [[23:161|IFH 6-28]]
Not anticipating what the instrument will show [[23:146|IFH 6-13]]; trust in reliable displays [[23:161|IFH 6-28]]
Watch the eyes: a gaze that never goes to an instrument signals inattention [[25:82|AIH 3-31]]
Emphasis
Altitude held by the attitude picture alone, close but not precise [[23:146|IFH 6-13]]
Relying on the instrument best understood [[23:146|IFH 6-13]]
Correct it early; it becomes a habit if not corrected [[23:161|IFH 6-28]]
Slowing the scan after a correction
Pitch drifts again while the student waits for it to settle
Cross-check and trim errors [[23:174|IFH 7-13]]
Keep cross-checking and trim off the pressures [[23:174|IFH 7-13]]

body.p: **Improper power control.**

head: Error
What you see
Usual cause
Fix and how to teach it
rows: Not knowing power settings and attitudes
Repeated power hunting after every change
No numbers for this airplane [[23:174|IFH 7-13]] [[23:206|IFH 7-45]]
Brief the POH settings; approximate settings make changes much easier [[23:170|IFH 7-9]]
Abrupt throttle
Yaw, roll and pitch jumps with each power change [[23:141|IFH 6-8]]
Throttle moved too fast; how far the airplane moves depends on how much and how rapidly the power is changed [[23:141|IFH 6-8]] [[23:174|IFH 7-13]]
Move the throttle by feel, then check the gauge [[23:137|IFH 6-4]]
Failure to lead the airspeed
Speed falls below target, then more adjustments
Power set only at the target speed [[23:174|IFH 7-13]]
Set the new power before the target speed; when leveling from a descent, add power early [[23:174|IFH 7-13]] [[23:206|IFH 7-45]]
Fixation on airspeed or manifold pressure
Erratic airspeed and power while altitude and heading slip
Staring at the gauge during the change [[23:174|IFH 7-13]]
A small power error matters less than large altitude and heading errors; staring does not slow the airplane [[23:174|IFH 7-13]]
Chasing the digital power number
Fiddling to the exact reading
Precision of glass readouts [[23:154|IFH 6-21]]
Set it, let it stabilize, avoid overcontrolling [[23:154|IFH 6-21]]

check.q: The examiner, flying, quietly eases the power back and holds altitude. As the speed decays he says, "I'm nose-high, so I'll push." What do you say?
check.a: That is insufficient cross-check and interpretation: the airspeed is low because power is low, not because the nose is high. Check the altimeter before deciding on pitch or power, then reset power [[23:173|IFH 7-12]] [[23:169|IFH 7-8]].

chunks.title: Common errors: corrections, coordination and trim

body.p: **Failure to make smooth, precise corrections, as required.**

head: Error
What you see
Usual cause
Fix and how to teach it
rows: Late corrections, accepted deviations
A 20 ft error left alone; 60 ft held because it is inside ±100 ft
Fear of overcontrolling; "it's within standards" [[23:173|IFH 7-12]] [[23:205|IFH 7-44]]
Practice small corrections and find the cause of overcontrolling; deviations are expected but not accepted [[23:173|IFH 7-12]] [[23:205|IFH 7-44]]
Overcontrolling pitch
VSI more than 200 fpm past the rate wanted; nose-high to nose-low swings [[23:139|IFH 6-6]] [[23:197|IFH 7-36]]
A large pitch change in a hurry [[23:165|IFH 7-4]] [[23:205|IFH 7-44]]
0.5° to 2° on glass, half or one bar on round dials, in two steps [[23:205|IFH 7-44]] [[23:165|IFH 7-4]]
Chasing the VSI
Pitch follows every needle swing
Not understanding the instrument [[23:173|IFH 7-12]]
Cross-check the other pitch instruments and explain lag [[23:173|IFH 7-12]] [[23:166|IFH 7-5]]
Improper bank for the heading error
A 10° error fixed with 20° of bank overshoots the heading
Bank not matched to the correction [[23:174|IFH 7-13]]
Bank no more than the degrees to turn [[23:168|IFH 7-7]]
Small heading errors tolerated
Heading creeps off a few degrees and stays
Zero error is not the goal [[23:174|IFH 7-13]]
A 1° error takes far less time and attention than a 20° error [[23:174|IFH 7-13]]

body.p: **Uncoordinated use of controls.**

head: Error
What you see
Usual cause
Fix and how to teach it
rows: Premature rudder
Ball off center before the heading moves
Anticipating heading changes [[23:174|IFH 7-13]]
Coordinated aileron and rudder, used together [[23:169|IFH 7-8]]
Power changes not countered
Heading drifts and ball moves when power changes
No rudder and aileron with the power change [[23:170|IFH 7-9]]
Faster cross-check with power changes; be ready with rudder [[23:170|IFH 7-9]] [[23:172|IFH 7-11]]
Slip or skid left uncorrected
Ball or slip/skid bar off center; on glass, roll pointer and index misaligned with a steady heading
Slip/skid indicator left out of the scan [[23:161|IFH 6-28]]
Rudder on the side of the ball or bar, then retrim [[23:169|IFH 7-8]] [[23:200|IFH 7-39]]

body.p: **Improper trim control.**

head: Error
What you see
Usual cause
Fix and how to teach it
rows: Faulty trim sequence
Attitude changed with the trim wheel; erratic control
Trim used in place of the controls [[23:174|IFH 7-13]] [[23:206|IFH 7-45]]
Hold the attitude first, then trim off the pressure [[23:206|IFH 7-45]]
Pitch correction not trimmed
Pitch drifts back during a distraction
No retrim after the pitch change [[23:205|IFH 7-44]]
Retrim after every pitch change and keep a fast cross-check [[23:205|IFH 7-44]]
Excessive trim
Pressures that must be held until fixed
Too much at once [[23:174|IFH 7-13]]
Trim often, in small amounts [[23:174|IFH 7-13]]
Repeated heading error
The same slight left turn corrected again and again
Left-wing-low trim condition ignored [[23:174|IFH 7-13]]
Find the cause and trim it out [[23:174|IFH 7-13]]
Misunderstood trim
Retrimming while the speed still changes; altitude wanders
Not knowing trim sets an airspeed [[23:206|IFH 7-45]]
Hold speed constant before final trim [[23:204|IFH 7-43]]
Seat and trim device problems
Tense ankles; trim rolled the wrong way in a new type
Seat or pedals badly set; trim devices differ [[23:174|IFH 7-13]]
Adjust seat and pedals; practice each type's trim on the ground (Application)

check.q: Your student corrects a 10° heading error with 20° of bank and overshoots. Name the error and the fix.
check.a: Correcting with improper bank: the airplane rolls past the heading before the bank is set and needs a correction the other way. Use a bank no greater than the degrees to turn [[23:174|IFH 7-13]] [[23:168|IFH 7-7]].

chunks.title: Building the lesson: briefing, practice and assessment

body.p: The PTS defines instructional knowledge as following the AIH's teaching methods [[FAA-S-8081-9E:10|PTS Use of the PTS]]. The AIH's demonstration-performance method has four phases: explanation, demonstration, student performance with instructor supervision, and evaluation [[25:175|AIH 9-5]].

head: Stage
What you do
rows: Explain on the ground
Objectives, completion standards, safety procedures and the end result; invite questions [[25:175|AIH 9-5]]
Build the blocks
Cross-check and interpretation are learned separately and in a deliberate sequence [[23:143|IFH 6-10]]; deliberate practice with brief, explicit feedback and no distractions [[25:77|AIH 3-26]]
Full panel, then partial panel
Pitch by the altimeter alone in VMC first [[23:165|IFH 7-4]]; then gyros covered [[23:162|IFH 7-1]]; on glass, the AHRS simulated [[23:194|IFH 7-33]]
Add load
Distractions only after the task works alone [[25:81|AIH 3-30]] [[25:180|AIH 9-10]]
Correct errors
Tell the student soon, and do not let mistakes be practiced [[25:76|AIH 3-25]]; safety permitting, let a student go part way into a mistake and find the way out [[25:182|AIH 9-12]]
Plateaus
Normal and temporary; move to a different task for a while [[25:77|AIH 3-26]]
Assess
Against standards for the student's stage, element by element [[25:182|AIH 9-12]]; collaborative assessment, the student's self-assessment first [[25:176|AIH 9-6]]

body.p: Check understanding, not only performance. If a student flies a maneuver well but may not understand it, have her vary it or combine it with another; a student who lacks the principles usually cannot [[25:182|AIH 9-12]]. Application: an airspeed change flown partial panel is a good test.

callout.text: Application: match the load to the stage. In the cognitive stage the student often fixates and distractions make performance fall apart [[25:75|AIH 3-24]]; save radio calls and chart work for later.

check.q: Your student flies partial panel straight-and-level perfectly in calm air. How do you check that she understands it?
check.a: Have her vary it or combine it with another maneuver, such as an airspeed change partial panel; students who do not understand the principles usually cannot do this [[25:182|AIH 9-12]].

body.p: In the telling-and-doing technique, you first demonstrate while explaining the power settings and attitudes, in the same order as the briefing; if the demo strays from the explanation, say so at once [[25:177|AIH 9-7]]. Next the student tells while you fly, so you can check her understanding before she is busy on the controls [[25:178|AIH 9-8]]. Avoid jargon the student does not know [[25:177|AIH 9-7]].
A full panel talk-through in primary-and-supporting words, flown to the instrument pilot skill level [[FAA-S-8081-9E:13|PTS Evaluator Responsibility]]:

bullets: "Cruise power is set from the POH, and after level-off I set the miniature airplane on the horizon bar at cruise [[23:138|IFH 6-5]]."

"Altimeter is primary for pitch, heading indicator for bank, airspeed for power. The attitude indicator supports pitch and bank, the VSI pitch, the turn coordinator bank, and the tach, our fixed-pitch power gauge, supports power [[23:170|IFH 7-9]]."
"My eyes come back through the attitude indicator between every other instrument [[23:144|IFH 6-11]]."
"Forty feet low and creeping: half a bar width up with light pressure, first to stop the needle, then about 80 feet per minute back up [[23:165|IFH 7-4]] [[23:166|IFH 7-5]]."
"On altitude: relax the pressure, check, and trim it off [[23:165|IFH 7-4]] [[23:143|IFH 6-10]]."
"Three degrees left of heading: about three degrees of bank, wings level when back on, ball centered [[23:168|IFH 7-7]] [[23:169|IFH 7-8]]."
"Airspeed five knots low with altitude steady: altimeter first, then power [[23:169|IFH 7-8]]."

body.p: The same flight in control-and-performance words: "I establish the level attitude and cruise power, trim, cross-check altimeter, airspeed and VSI, and adjust attitude or power on the control instruments [[23:135|IFH 6-2]] [[23:136|IFH 6-3]]."

Partial panel version, gyros covered: "Pitch now from the altimeter's rate of movement, the VSI and airspeed. Bank from the turn coordinator's airplane, ball centered. Heading from the compass in steady flight. Small, smooth inputs only [[23:165|IFH 7-4]] [[23:169|IFH 7-8]] [[23:183|IFH 7-22]] [[23:197|IFH 7-36]]." On glass with the AHRS failed: "Standby attitude indicator low in the panel, altitude tape and trend for pitch, compass for heading [[23:219|IFH 7-58]] [[23:197|IFH 7-36]]."

callout.text: Application: the PTS treats an explanation that needs prompting as a typical reason for an unsatisfactory [[FAA-S-8081-9E:15|PTS Unsatisfactory Performance]]. Rehearse this script aloud under the hood with a safety pilot until you can keep talking through a correction without the numbers drifting.

check.q: During your demo you drift 70 feet high while explaining. What does the AIH say to do?
check.a: Acknowledge and explain the deviation right away [[25:177|AIH 9-7]], then correct it as you teach: half a bar width down for about 140 fpm [[23:165|IFH 7-4]] [[23:166|IFH 7-5]].

scenario.title: Full panel to partial panel in a single-vacuum trainer
scenario.setup: You are a new CFII. Your instrument student, a commercial pilot, flies the school's fixed-pitch trainer: six-pack panel, one engine-driven vacuum pump for the attitude and heading indicators, an electric turn coordinator and no low-vacuum warning light. Next week she moves to the same model with a PFD and standby instruments. Today's plan is straight-and-level, full panel and then partial panel, in VMC with 6 miles in haze, in a practice area beside a busy airway. Her checkride is in three weeks.

questions.q: What do you brief before engine start that is specific to today's lesson?
questions.a: The three-step exchange of flight controls with a visual check [[25:178|AIH 9-8]]; that you are the lookout, since see and avoid still applies [[60:447|14 CFR 91.113(b)]] and haze near an airway calls for extra margin [[33:258|AIM 4-3-16]]; how you will simulate the failure, by covering the gyros [[23:162|IFH 7-1]]; and, as your own rule, that any real abnormality ends the exercise.

questions.q: Full panel, she keeps the attitude picture perfect, but the altitude drifts 80 feet over two minutes. Name it and fix it.
questions.a: Emphasis: the attitude indicator alone gives only reasonably close altitude; the altimeter must be in the cross-check [[23:146|IFH 6-13]]. Correct with half a bar width for about 160 fpm [[23:165|IFH 7-4]] [[23:166|IFH 7-5]].

questions.q: You cover the attitude and heading indicators. Within a minute she is 150 feet low, then 100 feet high, and 20° off heading. What is happening and what do you teach?
questions.a: Abrupt reactions to altitude changes set up an oscillation that can disorient her and fix her on the altimeter, costing heading [[23:197|IFH 7-36]]. Small inputs: stop the needle, then return [[23:165|IFH 7-4]]; keep the turn coordinator's airplane level with the ball centered [[23:169|IFH 7-8]].

questions.q: She asks why bother: "the vacuum pump never quits, and next week's airplane has glass." What do you answer?
questions.a: Pumps occasionally fail, and many small airplanes give no warning [[23:332|IFH 11-7]] [[23:333|IFH 11-8]]; the PTS stresses single vacuum sources for this reason [[FAA-S-8081-9E:16|PTS Emphasis on Attitude Instrument Flying and Partial Panel Skills]]. Glass has its own failures: an AHRS failure removes attitude and heading from the PFD [[23:217|IFH 7-56]], and backups may share pitot-static sources with the main display [[24:364|AFH 18-15]].

questions.q: Back on full panel you quietly pull the power back 100 rpm. She pushes the nose down as the speed decays. What do you say?
questions.a: What you see, the name, the cause, the fix: "Speed's low and we're descending. That's insufficient cross-check: the power is low, not the nose high. Check the altimeter first, then reset the power" [[23:173|IFH 7-12]] [[23:169|IFH 7-8]] [[23:205|IFH 7-44]].

questions.q: In the debrief, how do you assess her?
questions.a: Collaborative assessment: her self-assessment first, then yours, compared in discussion [[25:176|AIH 9-6]], judging each element against standards for her stage, not only the overall result [[25:182|AIH 9-12]].

skills.do: From the right seat, fly straight-and-level to the instrument pilot skill level while explaining, in your chosen method's words, the primary and supporting (or control and performance) instruments, the cross-check, each correction and the trim, first full panel and then partial panel or backup instruments on the panel you fly.
skills.practice: Rehearse the talk-through in the last chunk aloud under the hood with a qualified safety pilot [[60:446|14 CFR 91.109(c)(1)]], in the same order you brief it, admitting any deviation at once [[25:177|AIH 9-7]].

skills.do: When the evaluator flies a listed error, say what you see on the instruments, name the error, explain its cause and give the fix, then demonstrate the fix if asked.
skills.practice: Take turns with another applicant flying the IFH error lists for each other [[23:173|IFH 7-12]] [[23:174|IFH 7-13]] [[23:205|IFH 7-44]] [[23:206|IFH 7-45]], never simulating anything that could jeopardize safe flight [[FAA-S-8081-9E:10|PTS Use of the PTS]].

quiz.q: Your student asks why you call the altimeter "primary" for pitch when the attitude indicator sits in the middle of the panel. What does the IFH say?
options: The attitude indicator is too unreliable to be primary
Most pertinent information; usually held constant
The altimeter is primary in every phase of every flight
The checkride standards require you to call it primary
quiz.why: The primary instrument gives the most pertinent information for the maneuver and is usually the one held at a constant indication [[23:167|IFH 7-6]]. That does not devalue the attitude indicator, which should always be used when available [[23:143|IFH 6-10]], and the VSI becomes primary while returning to an altitude [[23:166|IFH 7-5]].

quiz.q: In the IFH slowdown from 120 to 100 knots, the throttle is pulled to about 15 inches. Which instrument is primary for power at that moment?
options: Airspeed indicator
Tachometer
Attitude indicator
Manifold pressure gauge
quiz.why: With the smooth reduction to about 15 inches, the manifold pressure gauge is momentarily primary for power. The airspeed indicator is primary again once power is reset near 100 knots, so it is the tempting but wrong answer for that moment [[23:170|IFH 7-9]] [[23:172|IFH 7-11]].

quiz.q: Your glass student is 60 feet low. Per IFH 7-36, what pitch change is a good start?
options: About 1°, a fifth of the chevron
About 5°, the chevron's full height
Whatever gives 500 fpm at once
Two full bar widths on the standby
quiz.why: For deviations under 100 feet, use about 1°, a fifth of the chevron's thickness [[23:197|IFH 7-36]]. The 500 fpm figure is a cap on the return rate, not a target [[23:155|IFH 6-22]].

quiz.q: This airplane's vacuum pump has failed. What is it actually doing, according to the IFH?
options: Turning left and descending slowly past 2,000 feet
Climbing in a shallow right turn
Level at 2,000 feet and not turning
Turning left at a standard rate
quiz.why: The airplane is level at 2,000 feet and not in a left turn; a pilot who misses the failure flags may misread the failed gyros [[23:332|IFH 11-7]]. The level turn coordinator and the VSI at zero agree with the altimeter.

quiz.q: Which quick comparison does the IFH give for finding a failed analog flight instrument?
options: Heading indicator against the magnetic compass alone
Airspeed indicator against tachometer and fuel flow
Altimeter against the field elevation
Attitude indicator against turn indicator and VSI
quiz.why: Immediately compare the attitude indicator with the rate-of-turn indicator and VSI. Besides pitch and bank, this compares the static system with the suction or pressure system and the electrical system [[23:332|IFH 11-7]]. The compass alone cannot check pitch.

quiz.q: Your student adds 50 rpm at 100 knots in level flight and changes nothing else. Per IFH 7-43, what happens?
options: It speeds up and stays faster at the same altitude
It climbs, then settles back at 100 knots higher up
It descends; power pitches the nose down
Nothing, since the trim holds the altitude
quiz.why: The airplane is trimmed for an airspeed, not an altitude: the extra speed makes extra lift, it climbs, and the airspeed settles at 100 knots again at a higher altitude [[23:204|IFH 7-43]].

quiz.q: On a PFD the heading is steady, but the roll pointer and roll index are not aligned. What is wrong and what is the fix?
options: AHRS failure; go to the standby
Gyro precession; wait a minute
Uncoordinated; apply rudder
Turbulence; average the readings
quiz.why: With a constant heading and the pointer and index misaligned, the airplane is uncoordinated; apply rudder [[23:200|IFH 7-39]]. Precession is not the answer: solid-state displays have eliminated precession error [[23:199|IFH 7-38]].

quiz.q: A student fixes every altitude error by rolling the trim wheel. Which IFH trim fault is this?
options: Faulty sequence, trim used in place of control
Excessive trim control, set in large amounts
Confusion over trim wheels that turn backward
Seat and pedals set so the ankles are tense
quiz.why: Trim should relieve pressures already held, not substitute for the controls [[23:174|IFH 7-13]] [[23:206|IFH 7-45]]. Using trim alone to change attitude leads to erratic control [[23:173|IFH 7-12]].

quiz.q: What reason does the CFII PTS give for its emphasis on partial panel skills?
options: Most training airplanes now have dual vacuum systems
Fatal disorientation with failed gyros or displays
Partial panel replaces unusual attitudes on the test
Glass displays fail more often than round dials do
quiz.why: The PTS cites fatal spatial disorientation accidents of instrument-rated pilots flying with failed gyros or a lost electronic display, and notes that many light airplanes have only a single vacuum source [[FAA-S-8081-9E:16|PTS Emphasis on Attitude Instrument Flying and Partial Panel Skills]]. Glass is not the weak link: solid-state instruments fail far less often than analog ones [[23:149|IFH 6-16]]. Task H is always required, so nothing is replaced [[FAA-S-8081-9E:32|PTS Area VI NOTE]].

quiz.q: Your student holds altitude 60 feet off and says it is inside the ±100 foot standard. What does the IFH call this, and what is the fix?
options: Good judgment; it avoids overcontrolling the airplane
Emphasis; fly the attitude indicator more
Late trim; retrim before correcting
Acceptance of deviations; correct promptly
quiz.why: The IFH uses this example: deviations should be expected but not accepted, so cross-check and correct promptly [[23:205|IFH 7-44]]. Leaving a small error alone for fear of overcontrolling is the listed late-correction fault, not good judgment [[23:173|IFH 7-12]].

quiz.q: Your glass student's PFD has failed. Why will flying these standby instruments feel harder than flying the PFD?
options: They need a working AHRS to show any pitch at all
They show bank but give no pitch information
They are small and not directly in front of her
They work only while the alternator runs
quiz.why: The standby airspeed indicator, attitude indicator and altimeter sit low in the center panel [[23:332|IFH 11-7]], the kind of backup the PTS says may not be directly in front of the pilot [[FAA-S-8081-9E:16|PTS Emphasis on Attitude Instrument Flying and Partial Panel Skills]]. They need no electrical power or have their own battery [[23:149|IFH 6-16]], so they do not depend on the AHRS or the alternator.

quiz.q: Your trainer's VSI reads 100 fpm down in level flight and cannot be adjusted. What does the IFH say?
options: Treat that reading as the zero
Cover it and fly without it
Hold 100 fpm up to cancel it
Use it only for climbs and descents
quiz.why: If the VSI cannot be readjusted, allow for the error: a 100 fpm descent reading in level flight becomes the zero, and any change from it shows a pitch change [[23:139|IFH 6-6]] [[23:166|IFH 7-5]].

final_quiz.q: A student trained elsewhere says control and performance and primary and supporting need different control movements. What do you tell her?
options: Right; one method uses trim and the other does not
Right; primary and supporting ignores the attitude gyro
Same instruments and the same control responses
They match on glass but differ on round dials
final_quiz.why: Both methods use the same instruments and responses; they differ only in reliance on the attitude indicator and how other instruments are interpreted [[23:135|IFH 6-2]] [[23:149|IFH 6-16]]. Primary and supporting does not devalue the attitude indicator [[23:143|IFH 6-10]].

final_quiz.q: Your glass student is 200 feet low. Per IFH 7-36, what return rate makes sense?
options: 200 fpm
400 fpm
800 fpm
final_quiz.why: Use a rate about double the deviation, never more than the optimum climb or descent rate: 200 feet off calls for 400 fpm [[23:197|IFH 7-36]]. The IFH's 1,400 fpm figure is for a 700-foot error and is beyond most airplanes [[23:198|IFH 7-37]].

final_quiz.q: Partial panel on round dials, the altimeter needle moves rapidly clockwise. What does that tell your student?
options: A small nose-high pitch error
A large nose-low pitch error
A blocked static port
A large nose-high pitch error
final_quiz.why: A rapid clockwise needle means a considerable nose-high deviation, while a slow counterclockwise movement means slightly nose-low [[23:165|IFH 7-4]]. A blocked static port would freeze the altimeter instead [[23:98|IFH 5-3]].

final_quiz.q: Flying east partial panel, your student speeds up from 90 to 110 knots and the compass swings toward north. What do you teach?
options: Acceleration error; keep the wings level
A real left turn: roll right until it stops
Compass failure: switch to timed turns now
Turning error: lead by the latitude
final_quiz.why: On an east or west heading, acceleration gives a north turn indication and deceleration a south turn indication [[23:183|IFH 7-22]]. Keep the turn coordinator's airplane level [[23:168|IFH 7-7]] and read the compass once the speed is steady. Rolling right would create a real turn.

final_quiz.q: In the IFH example system, what does an AHRS failure take away?
options: Only the airspeed and altitude tapes on the PFD
Only the moving map and engine page on the MFD
Attitude, heading and unusual attitude protection
Nothing, since the display simply reverts to the MFD
final_quiz.why: An AHRS failure removes all heading and attitude indications on the PFD and all unusual attitude protection, and the autopilot keeps only roll and altitude hold [[23:217|IFH 7-56]]. The altimeter and VSI tape still work in that failure, which is why they become the pitch reference [[23:217|IFH 7-56]].

final_quiz.q: After a roll-out on round dials, the heading keeps changing while the attitude indicator shows wings level and the ball is centered. What is going on?
options: A skid; add rudder on the side of the ball
Turning; the attitude gyro has precessed
Normal drift from Earth's rotation
Turbulence; average out the readings
final_quiz.why: If the heading indicator shows a change while the attitude indicator shows level flight, the airplane is turning; with the ball centered, the attitude gyro has precessed [[23:186|IFH 7-25]]. A centered ball rules out a skid, and Earth-rate drift is only about 15° per hour [[23:115|IFH 5-20]].

final_quiz.q: This PFD shows the airspeed falling at 18 inches and 1800 RPM after the pilot lowered the nose. Which error does the IFH show?
options: Chasing the VSI in turbulent air
Fixation on the heading trend vector
Faulty trim sequence after leveling from a climb
Insufficient cross-check: power, not pitch
final_quiz.why: The IFH says the problem is power, not a nose-high attitude, so lowering the nose was wrong. Increase the cross-check of all supporting instruments and stabilize airspeed and altitude before an input [[23:204|IFH 7-43]] [[23:205|IFH 7-44]].

final_quiz.q: In this figure the pilot made a pitch correction and is watching the altimeter. What error is shown, and what is the fix?
options: Fixation; keep the whole scan going
Omission of the standby; check the backup gyro
Overcontrolling; use half-degree pitch steps
Accepted deviation; correct the altitude now
final_quiz.why: Fixation during cross-check: all attention went to pitch and altitude while the heading began to change. Monitor all instruments and do not fixate while waiting for a correction to show [[23:205|IFH 7-44]] [[23:206|IFH 7-45]].

final_quiz.q: Your student asks what the pitch trim actually sets. What does the IFH say?
options: A specific altitude
A specific pitch attitude
A specific airspeed
A specific power setting
final_quiz.why: An aircraft is trimmed for a specific airspeed, not a pitch attitude or altitude, so any airspeed change needs retrimming [[23:204|IFH 7-43]]. Not understanding this is a listed trim error [[23:206|IFH 7-45]].

final_quiz.q: What is the main benefit of the "student tells, instructor does" step of telling-and-doing?
options: She gets more hands-on time on the flight controls
She sorts out the steps; you check understanding
The examiner can grade your flying as she talks
It lets you skip the preflight briefing entirely
final_quiz.why: Freed from flying, the student organizes her thoughts about the steps, and the instructor can evaluate her understanding before she is absorbed in controlling the airplane [[25:178|AIH 9-8]]. She is not on the controls in this step.

final_quiz.q: Your student starts to let the altitude go during a chart task. It is VMC, high and clear of traffic. What does AIH 9-12 suggest?
options: Take the controls the moment the first error shows
Say nothing until the debrief, then list all her errors
Add two more distractions to raise the challenge
If safe, let her go part way in and find a way out
final_quiz.why: Correcting errors does not mean taking over at once; safety permitting, it is often better to let learners progress part way into a mistake and find a way out [[25:182|AIH 9-12]]. Do not let the mistake be practiced into a habit, though [[25:76|AIH 3-25]].

final_quiz.q: During your demo, the examiner has to prompt you twice before your explanation is complete. How does the PTS view that?
options: It is a typical reason for an unsatisfactory
It is noted, but only the flying itself is graded
It is fine if the numbers stayed in limits
The examiner simply repeats the Task
final_quiz.why: The PTS lists failure to give a clear, concise, technically accurate and complete explanation without prompting as a typical reason for an unsatisfactory [[FAA-S-8081-9E:15|PTS Unsatisfactory Performance]]. The AIH has the instructor explain while demonstrating, in the same sequence as the briefing [[25:177|AIH 9-7]].

final_quiz.q: Your glass student works hard to hold airspeed within 1 knot and drifts off altitude. What does the IFH say?
options: Good: the tape is precise enough to hold it
Make the airspeed trend the main reference
No need: the standards allow more latitude
Hold it with power alone, never with pitch
final_quiz.why: Fixation can lead to holding airspeed to an unnecessarily tight tolerance; there is no need to hold it to one knot [[23:161|IFH 6-28]]. Trend vectors are a supplement, not the primary reference [[23:160|IFH 6-27]].

final_quiz.q: Which instrument does the IFH name as one of the most commonly omitted from the glass scan?
options: The altitude tape
Slip/skid indicator
The attitude display
The airspeed tape
final_quiz.why: Pilots tend to omit the standby instruments and compass, and one of the most commonly omitted instruments is the slip/skid indicator [[23:161|IFH 6-28]]. The attitude display is hard to miss, since part of it is always in view [[23:157|IFH 6-24]].

final_quiz.q: Your trainer has a vacuum system and no low-vacuum warning light. What do you teach?
options: Rely on the gyro flags alone
Fly IMC only with autopilot on
Check suction only before takeoff
Keep the suction gauge in the scan
final_quiz.why: Many small airplanes have no vacuum warning, so the pilot should monitor the vacuum or pressure gauge [[23:332|IFH 11-7]] [[23:333|IFH 11-8]]; some airplanes have only the gauge [[1:224|PHAK 8-22]]. A pilot can also miss the off or failure flags [[23:332|IFH 11-7]].

final_quiz.q: Your student's heading slides left after every correction, flight after flight. What does the IFH tell you to look for?
options: A left-wing-low out-of-trim condition
A heading indicator drifting 15° per hour
An attitude indicator set too low for cruise
A VSI that is out of calibration
final_quiz.why: Failing to note the cause of a heading error means repeating it: the IFH example is a left-wing-low trim condition corrected again and again while the trim is ignored [[23:174|IFH 7-13]].

final_quiz.q: Before departure in a glass trainer, what does the IFH say should be set so the standby battery can take over the essential bus after a charging failure?
options: Avionics master switched off
Alternate static source open
Standby battery in ARM
Autopilot set to roll mode
final_quiz.why: Generally the standby battery switch must be in ARM for the standby battery to come online, and arming should be done before departure; the AFM has the specifics [[23:331|IFH 11-6]].

takeaways: Pick one method for the checkride, but know both: same instruments, same hands, different words.
Level flight: altimeter for pitch, heading for bank, airspeed for power; the VSI is primary while returning to altitude.
Altitude and airspeed off in opposite directions: pitch alone may fix both. Both off the same way: pitch and power.
Round dials: half a bar under 100 feet, a full bar over. Glass: about 1°. Return at double the error, within limits.
Partial panel: altimeter rate, turn coordinator and ball, compass in steady flight, small smooth inputs.
On glass, know what an AHRS failure takes away and where the standby instruments sit.
Trim sets an airspeed: pressure first, then trim, and retrim after every change.
For every error: what you see, its name, its cause, the fix and how you would show it.
cfi_notes: The IFH gives several pitch-size rules. Chapter 6 says one correction should not exceed half a bar width [[23:138|IFH 6-5]]; Chapter 7 allows an initial full bar width over 100 feet [[23:165|IFH 7-4]]; the glass pages give about 1° under 100 feet [[23:197|IFH 7-36]] and 0.5° to 2° by severity [[23:205|IFH 7-44]]. Teach the one that matches the panel and say why they differ.

Return-rate limits also differ: never more than the optimum rate on round dials [[23:166|IFH 7-5]], not over 500 fpm in IFH 6-22 [[23:155|IFH 6-22]], and an optimum of 500 to 1,000 fpm in IFH 7-37 [[23:198|IFH 7-37]]. All agree on double the error for small deviations.

Which instrument is primary for pitch is not fixed: the IFH normally uses the altimeter but says it depends on airplane, weather and pilot [[23:167|IFH 7-6]], and on glass calls the attitude indicator primary only when flying a specific pitch or bank angle [[23:199|IFH 7-38]]. Examiners like to ask this.

The PTS lists FAA-H-8083-9, FAA-H-8083-15 and FAA-S-ACS-8 without suffixes [[FAA-S-8081-9E:32|PTS VI.A]]; teach from the current AIH (9B) and IFH (15B). The IFH itself still refers to the Instrument Rating PTS [[23:161|IFH 6-28]] [[23:205|IFH 7-44]]; the instrument standard is now the Instrument Rating ACS [[FAA-S-ACS-8C:3|IR ACS Revision History]].

IFH 7-7 ends its turn coordinator paragraph by saying "the turn-and-slip indicator provides both roll and turn indications" [[23:168|IFH 7-7]], but IFH 6-8 and 7-8 say the turn-and-slip indicator shows turn rate only and the turn coordinator shows roll and turn [[23:141|IFH 6-8]] [[23:169|IFH 7-8]]. Teach the turn coordinator as the instrument that shows roll rate.

The PTS names the view-limiting device for Task H and the nonprecision approach (Area VIII, Task A) [[FAA-S-8081-9E:10|PTS Use of the PTS]]. For this Task, agree with the examiner beforehand whether you will wear it, and brief when and how it goes on and off; on the test it must not block the examiner's view [[60:225|14 CFR 61.45(d)(2)]].

The AIH pulls two ways on errors: do not let learners practice mistakes [[25:76|AIH 3-25]], yet safety permitting let them go part way into a mistake and find the way out [[25:182|AIH 9-12]]. Use the second for understanding and the first for habits.

The IFH glass failure pages show one example system, with no standby turn coordinator and a roll mode fed by a hidden turn coordinator [[23:217|IFH 7-56]] [[23:219|IFH 7-58]]. Teach failures from the AFM supplement of the airplane you fly.

Expect the examiner to ask for the primary and supporting instruments in level flight and during an airspeed change, what replaces each failed gyro, and to fly the power-caused airspeed loss from IFH 7-12 [[23:173|IFH 7-12]]. The PTS also requires a realistic distraction during the flight [[FAA-S-8081-9E:16|PTS Use of Distractions During Practical Tests]].
gaps: The CFII PTS gives no numeric tolerances for this Task; it asks for the instrument pilot skill level [[FAA-S-8081-9E:13|PTS Evaluator Responsibility]]. The Instrument Rating ACS standard is altitude ±100 feet in level flight, selected headings ±10°, airspeed ±10 knots and bank ±5° in turns [[FAA-S-ACS-8C:16|IR ACS IR.IV.A.S1]] (the Instrument lesson IR.IV.A teaches them); the IFH quotes the same ±100 feet [[23:205|IFH 7-44]].
Pitch attitudes, power settings and trim feel for level flight at each speed come from the POH/AFM and practice; the IFH uses a sample retractable airplane [[23:162|IFH 7-1]].
No source here says how to simulate an AHRS, ADC or display failure in a particular glass airplane (covers, reversionary mode or circuit breakers); follow the AFM supplement and school procedures.
No source gives the standby attitude indicator's battery endurance or says which instruments share pitot-static ports in a given airplane; that is in the AFM [[24:364|AFH 18-15]].
No source sets a minimum amount of partial panel training or a schedule for recurrent partial panel practice.

activities.title: Pitch, power or both?
activities.intro: Tap each picture, then tap the correction the IFH points to.

items.t: Altitude 100 ft high, airspeed 10 knots low
Altitude 80 ft low, airspeed 8 knots high
Altitude 100 ft high, airspeed 10 knots high
Altitude 100 ft low, airspeed 10 knots low
Altitude on target, airspeed 10 knots low and steady
Altitude on target, airspeed creeping up at the same attitude

activities.why: Opposite errors: pitch alone may fix both. Same-direction errors: pitch and power [[23:170|IFH 7-9]]. Any power change also needs elevator pressure to hold altitude [[23:170|IFH 7-9]]. With altitude constant, power decides airspeed, so check the altimeter first [[23:169|IFH 7-8]]. A rising airspeed in level flight suggests power has increased: adjust power or retrim [[23:141|IFH 6-8]].

activities.title: Name the primary
activities.intro: Tap a flight condition, then the instrument the IFH makes primary for it.

pairs.l: Pitch while returning to an altitude
Power while the throttle is pulled to the underpower setting

activities.why: Level flight primaries [[23:170|IFH 7-9]]; VSI while returning to altitude [[23:166|IFH 7-5]]; manifold pressure momentarily primary during the reduction [[23:172|IFH 7-11]]; slip/skid primary for yaw [[23:156|IFH 6-23]].

activities.title: Partial panel: who does which job now?
activities.intro: The vacuum pump has failed. Drag each label to its numbered pin on the panel.

pins.label: Failed gyro: cover it so it cannot mislead
Also vacuum-driven here: cover it, use compass and clock
Pitch: the needle's rate shows the size of the error
Shows the trend of a pitch change first
Power in level flight; a fast change means a big pitch change
Bank: keep its airplane level and the ball centered
Suction gauge: the only warning in many airplanes
Power gauge: not upset by turbulence or poor trim

activities.why: Failed vacuum attitude and heading indicators, covered [[23:332|IFH 11-7]]; altimeter rate and VSI trend [[23:165|IFH 7-4]]; airspeed [[23:167|IFH 7-6]] [[23:143|IFH 6-10]]; turn coordinator and ball [[23:168|IFH 7-7]] [[23:169|IFH 7-8]]; suction gauge [[23:333|IFH 11-8]]; power instruments [[23:137|IFH 6-4]]; compass and timed turns [[23:182|IFH 7-21]].

activities.title: When an analog gyro starts to lie
activities.intro: Put the IFH steps for an instrument failure in order, first to last, then tap Check.
steps: Keep control and speed up the cross-check to include all flight instruments
Compare the attitude indicator with the turn indicator and VSI
Identify the failed part and fly on the instruments that still work
Try to restore it: power source, backup or alternate system, reset
Advise ATC and, if needed, declare an emergency

activities.title: True or false: setting up the lesson safely
activities.intro: Decide whether each statement is true or false.

cards.s: On the CFII practical test you choose the method for Area VI, and the evaluator should determine that you fully understand it.
cards.why: True [[FAA-S-8081-9E:32|PTS Area VI NOTE]] [[FAA-S-8081-9E:17|PTS Emphasis on Attitude Instrument Flying and Partial Panel Skills]]. Both methods use the same instruments and control responses [[23:135|IFH 6-2]].

cards.s: To make the test realistic, the evaluator may simulate any error, even one that could put the airplane at risk.
cards.why: False. The PTS says the evaluator will not simulate any condition that may jeopardize safe flight [[FAA-S-8081-9E:10|PTS Use of the PTS]]; the AFH adds that some failure modes cannot be simulated in training [[24:372|AFH 18-23]].

cards.s: For simulated instrument training in your airplane, the safety pilot in the other control seat must hold at least a private pilot certificate with category and class ratings appropriate to the aircraft.
cards.why: True [[60:446|14 CFR 91.109(c)(1)(i)]]. The only other option in the rule is a sport pilot instructor giving training for a solo cross-country endorsement [[60:446|14 CFR 91.109(c)(1)(ii)]]. The safety pilot also needs adequate vision forward and to each side, or a competent observer [[60:447|14 CFR 91.109(c)(2)]].

cards.s: Once the student is under the view-limiting device on an IFR flight plan, see and avoid is ATC's job.
cards.why: False. When weather permits, each person operating an aircraft keeps watch to see and avoid, whether under IFR or VFR [[60:447|14 CFR 91.113(b)]].

cards.s: The exchange of flight controls is a three-step process, and a visual check is recommended.

activities.title: Numbers you will coach
activities.intro: Work it out, then type your answer.

items.q: Round dials: your student is 80 feet low. Using the IFH rule of thumb, what rate of return should the VSI show?
items.why: About double the altitude error: 2 x 80 = 160 fpm [[23:166|IFH 7-5]].

items.q: You want to return to altitude at 400 fpm. Above what VSI reading is your student overcontrolling?
items.why: Overcontrolling is more than 200 fpm past the rate wanted: 400 + 200 = 600 fpm [[23:198|IFH 7-37]] [[23:139|IFH 6-6]].

items.q: A free gyro heading indicator drifts 15° per hour from Earth's rotation alone. Not reset for 20 minutes, how far can it be off?
Partial panel, the student is 30° off heading. In a standard-rate timed turn, how many seconds of turn does she need?
items.why: Standard rate is 3° per second, so 30° / 3 = 10 seconds; with equal roll-in and roll-out rates, the roll time need not be counted [[23:182|IFH 7-21]].

activities.title: A partial panel lesson, one call at a time
activities.intro: Your instrument student flies a six-pack trainer with one vacuum pump and an electric turn coordinator. It is VMC and you are the safety pilot.

steps.s: On the ground she asks what to do first if the attitude indicator starts disagreeing with the other instruments in cloud.
options: Keep control, speed up the scan and compare it with the turn indicator and VSI
Reset the gyro with the caging knob and keep flying the attitude indicator
Call ATC first, then look at the instruments once the frequency is quiet
Engage the autopilot and let it fly on the attitude gyro until it settles
steps.why: Keep control while identifying the failure, expedite the cross-check and compare the attitude indicator with the rate-of-turn indicator and VSI; advising ATC comes after [[23:332|IFH 11-7]].

steps.s: You cover the attitude and heading indicators. She makes big pitch corrections and the altimeter swings 150 feet each way.
options: Tell her to use bigger, quicker inputs to catch it sooner
Uncover the attitude indicator until she settles down
Small, smooth inputs: stop the needle first, then return
Have her chase the VSI, since it reacts first
steps.why: Abrupt reactions cause larger pitch changes and oscillation; make small inputs, first stopping the needle, then returning to altitude [[23:197|IFH 7-36]] [[23:165|IFH 7-4]]. Chasing the VSI is itself a listed error [[23:173|IFH 7-12]].

steps.s: Her pitch settles, but the heading drifts 15° while she stares at the altimeter.
options: It is compass error; ignore the heading until the compass settles
Have her stop watching the altimeter and fly heading only
End partial panel for today; heading control comes later
Fixation on the altimeter is costing heading; widen the scan to the turn coordinator
steps.why: Fixation on the altimeter can cost directional control [[23:197|IFH 7-36]]. Keep the turn coordinator's airplane level for straight flight [[23:168|IFH 7-7]] and keep the whole scan going [[23:205|IFH 7-44]].

steps.s: You ask for a 20-knot slowdown on a westerly heading. As she slows, the compass swings toward south.
options: Real turn: roll toward north until the compass stops
Deceleration error: hold wings level on the turn coordinator
Compass failure: switch to timed turns right away
Heading indicator precession: reset it to the compass
steps.why: On an east or west heading, deceleration gives a south turn indication [[23:183|IFH 7-22]]. The turn coordinator shows whether she is really turning [[23:168|IFH 7-7]].

steps.s: In the debrief she says the flight went badly. You want her to own the lesson and improve.
options: Give her a letter grade and a list of every error
Skip the debrief and simply repeat the flight next week
Tell her the examiner will be easier on the checkride
Start with her self-assessment, then compare yours in discussion
steps.why: Collaborative assessment starts with the learner's self-assessment, followed by a discussion comparing it with the instructor's assessment [[25:176|AIH 9-6]] [[25:182|AIH 9-12]].

activities.title: Name that error
activities.intro: Tap what you see, then the error the IFH names for it.

pairs.l: Airspeed low; the student pushes the nose down and altitude drops
pairs.r: Insufficient cross-check: low power was the cause

pairs.l: Altitude 60 ft off and steady; no correction made
VSI at 700 fpm on a planned 400 fpm return
The same slight left turn corrected again and again
Speed drops below target because power came in late
Rudder pushed before the heading starts to change
